summary: Defines the Network Access Identifier, a standard syntax for the user identifier a client submits when asking for network access, typically in the form user@realm. It supports roaming and inter-domain authentication, and is a revision of an earlier specification.

plainLanguage.summary: When you log in to a hotel's wireless network, the hotel has to send a check to the company that gave you your account. The Network Access Identifier is the name that tells it where to send it, in the form user@example.com. RFC 7542 defines that format properly, including how it handles names with characters outside ASCII.

subtitle: The user@realm format for identifying who is asking for network access, so requests can be routed to the right home domain.

tldr.problem: Inter-domain authentication, or roaming, needs a standard way for one domain to identify another domain's users so a request can reach the user's home authentication server.
tldr.mechanism: The Network Access Identifier is a UTF-8 string of the form username@realm, with a formal ABNF grammar. The realm is a domain name used to route the request through AAA systems.
tldr.outcome: RFC 7542 revises RFC 4282, fixing its handling of international character sets, and recommends the NAI format for user identifiers in other protocols.

today: RFC 7542 is a Proposed Standard published in May 2015 that obsoletes RFC 4282, and no later RFC is recorded as obsoleting or updating it. The RFC lists the differences from its predecessor in its appendix.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
Considerable interest exists for a set of features that fit within the general category of inter-domain authentication, or roaming capability for network access, including dialup Internet users, Virtual Private Network usage, wireless LAN authentication and other applications. Inter-domain authentication refers to situations where a user has authentication credentials at one home domain but is able to present them at a second visited domain to access certain services there. The two domains generally have a pre-existing relationship, so that the credentials can be passed from the visited domain to the home domain for verification. The home domain typically responds with a permit or deny response, which may also include authorization parameters that the visited domain is expected to enforce on the user.

Interested parties include regional Internet service providers combining their efforts to offer dialup service over a wider area, telecommunications companies offering access in areas with no native service, wireless LAN hotspots serving one or more providers, and businesses offering employees a package of dialup services on a global basis, including secure access to corporate intranets through tunnelling protocols.

In order to enhance the interoperability of these services, it is necessary to have a standardized method for identifying users, and this document defines syntax for the Network Access Identifier. When the NAI was defined for network access, it had the side effect of defining an identifier that could be used in non-AAA systems. Some non-AAA systems defined compatible identifiers and deployments used the NAI, which simplified the management of credentials by reusing the same credential in multiple situations. There are privacy implications to using one identifier across multiple protocols.

The goal of the document is to define the format of an identifier that can be used in many protocols. A protocol may transport an encoded version of the NAI, but the definition of the NAI is protocol independent. The document only suggests that the NAI format be used; it does not require such use, and it makes no requirements on protocol specifications, implementations or deployments. Where identifiers need to be used in new protocols it is RECOMMENDED that the NAI format be used, because the interpretation of the identifier is context specific while the format stays the same. The recommendation for a standard identifier format is not a recommendation that each user have one universal identifier; the document allows multiple identifiers and recommends anonymous identifiers where those are publicly visible. This document is a revised version of RFC 4282.
sections.plainLanguage: The point of the format is that one identifier works everywhere, so a company does not have to invent a new account name for every network its staff use. The RFC only recommends the format; it does not force anything on other protocols.

sections.title: Motivation
sections.content:
The motivation to revise RFC 4282 began with internationalization concerns raised in the context of eduroam. RFC 4282 defined ABNF for realms and limited the realm grammar to English letters, digits and the hyphen character. The intent appears to have been to encode, compare and transport realms with the Punycode encoding form described in RFC 5891, and that approach had a number of problems.

The ABNF was not aligned with internationalization of DNS. The requirement that realms be ASCII conflicts with EAP and RADIUS, which are both 8-bit clean and which both recommend the use of UTF-8 for identifiers. The mappings required by RFC 4282 were language specific and nearly impossible for intermediate nodes to perform correctly without information about that language. The requirement to normalize usernames may conflict with local system or administrative requirements, and the recommendations for handling bidirectional characters proved unworkable. The prohibition of unassigned code points effectively prohibits support for new scripts. And no AAA client, proxy or server had implemented any of the requirements in that section.

With international roaming growing in popularity, it is important that these issues are corrected in order to provide robust and interoperable network services. The document was also motivated by a desire to codify existing practice related to the use of the NAI format and to encourage its widespread use.
sections.plainLanguage: The older version assumed realms were plain English names and had servers convert them to an encoded form. That is hard to do correctly in the middle of a network, and no one had managed to implement it.

sections.title: Formal Syntax
sections.content:
The grammar for the NAI is given in Augmented Backus-Naur Form. An NAI is a username on its own, a realm on its own, or a username followed by an at sign and a realm. The username is a dot-string, that is one or more strings separated by dots, and each string is made of one or more UTF-8 atext characters, which are letters, digits, a set of punctuation marks, and the extra characters that UTF-8 adds.

The realm is one or more labels separated by dots. Each label starts with a UTF-8 rtext character, which is a letter, a digit or an extra UTF-8 character, and continues with any number of rtext characters or hyphens, ending on an rtext character. That last rule is the familiar rule for a DNS label: a hyphen is allowed in the middle but not at the start or the end.

The RFC prints examples of valid identifiers, including bob, joe@example.com, fred@foo-9.example.com, jack@3rd.depts.example.com, fred.smith@example.com, fred_smith@example.com, fred$@example.com, nancy@eng.example.net, eng.example.net!nancy@example.net, eng%nancy@example.net and @privatecorp.example.net. Examples of invalid identifiers include fred@example, fred@example_9.com, fred@example.net@example.net, fred.@example.net, eng:nancy@example.net and (user)@example.net.
sections.plainLanguage: The name is a username, an at sign and a domain, and the domain has to look like a normal domain name. The username can be left out, and it can contain characters outside ASCII.

sections.title: Support for Username Privacy
sections.content:
Interpretation of the username part of the NAI depends on the realm in question, so the username portion SHOULD be treated as opaque data by nodes that are not part of the home domain for that realm. Only the home domain is capable of interpreting the meaning of the username portion; any third-party domain cannot form conclusions about it or decode it into subfields. It may be used as firstname.lastname, it may be entirely digits, or it may be a random hex identifier.

In some situations NAIs are used together with a separate authentication method that can transfer the username part in a more secure manner. In this case NAIs MAY be provided in an abbreviated form by omitting the username part. Omitting the username part is RECOMMENDED over using a fixed username such as anonymous, since including a fixed username is ambiguous as to whether the NAI refers to a single user, although current practice is to use the name anonymous instead of omitting the username part, and that behaviour is also permitted.

The most common use case for omitting or obfuscating the username part is with TLS-based EAP methods such as Tunneled Transport Layer Security. Those methods allow for an outer identifier, typically an anonymous at-realm, which routes the authentication request from a visited domain to a home domain while keeping the username part confidential from the visited network. The protocol then provides for an inner authentication exchange in which a full identifier is used.

Protocols that do not support such inner and outer exchanges are limited to an identifier that is publicly visible, and for those it is RECOMMENDED to use ephemeral identifiers. There may also be situations where portions of the realm are sensitive, and it is RECOMMENDED that the sensitive portion of the realm be omitted as well, for example using at example.com instead of at sensitive.example.com. The home domain is authoritative for users in all subdomains and can route the request to the appropriate subsystem within it. For roaming purposes it is typically necessary to locate the appropriate backend authentication server before the conversation can proceed, so authentication routing is impossible unless the realm portion is available and in a well-known format.
sections.plainLanguage: The part before the at sign says nothing to anyone except the home domain, so it can be left out when the network connection is protected. The domain part has to stay, because it is what routes the request home.

sections.title: The Normalization Process
sections.content:
Conversion to Unicode as well as normalization SHOULD be performed by edge systems such as laptops, desktops and smart phones that take local text as input. Those edge systems are best suited to determine the user's intent and to convert local text into a normalized form. Other AAA systems such as proxies do not have access to locale and character set information, so they may not always be able to convert local input to Unicode.

Inside an AAA system, NAIs are sent over the wire in their canonical form, and that canonical form is used for all NAI and realm comparisons. Strings that are not in Normal Form Composed are not valid NAIs and SHOULD NOT be treated as such. Implementations that expect an NAI but receive a non-normalized string SHOULD attempt to create a local version of the NAI that is normalized from the input identifier, and that local version MUST NOT be used outside the local context.

These requirements are not implemented today. Most EAP implementations use a user identifier passed to them from some other local system, treated as an opaque blob and placed as is into the EAP Identity field, and that blob can contain localized text, which means the AAA systems have to process it. In practice edge systems generally do not normalize the NAI, so AAA systems SHOULD attempt to normalize it. Where the identifier can be normalized, the normal form MUST be used as the NAI. In all other circumstances the identifier MUST NOT be treated as an NAI, but AAA systems MUST NOT fail authentication simply because the identifier is not an NAI.

When the realm portion of an NAI is not recognized by an AAA server, it SHOULD try to normalize the NAI into Normal Form Composed and use that to see whether the realm matches a known realm. If no match is found, the original form SHOULD be used in all subsequent processing. The server may also convert realms to Punycode and perform all realm comparisons on the resulting strings, though that may have different operational effects and failure modes.
sections.plainLanguage: Text typed on one computer and text typed on another can look identical and still differ in their internal encoding. The rule is that the machine the person is sitting at does the tidying up, because only it knows the language and keyboard the person used.

sections.title: Routing inside AAA Systems
sections.content:
Many AAA systems use the realm portion of the NAI to route requests within a proxy network. The semantics involve a logical AAA routing table in which the realm acts as a key and the values stored in the table are one or more next hop AAA servers. Intermediate nodes MUST use the realm portion of the NAI without modification to perform this lookup, and because they may not have the same locale information as the system that injected the NAI, almost all case-insensitive comparisons can be wrong. Where the realm is entirely ASCII, current AAA systems sometimes perform case-insensitive matching, and this method MAY be continued, since it has been shown to work in practice.

Many existing non-AAA systems have identifiers similar in format to the NAI but not compliant with this specification, for example using non-Normal-Form-Composed form or multiple at signs. Intermediate nodes SHOULD normalize such identifiers to Normal Form Composed before looking up the realm in the logical routing table, and MUST NOT modify the identifiers that they forward. The data as entered by the user is inviolate.

It is RECOMMENDED to use the entirety of the realm for routing decisions, although AAA systems MAY use part of it so long as that part is a valid realm. Routing fred@example.com to a com destination is forbidden, because com is not a valid realm, while routing fred@sales.example.com to the example.com destination is permissible. A single label such as fred@sales is forbidden as well, because many non-AAA systems treat a single label as a local identifier within their realm.

The home realm usually appears in the realm portion of the NAI, but in some cases a different realm can be used, for instance when the home realm is reachable only through intermediate proxies. NAIs MUST NOT use a different realm than the home realm unless the sender has explicit knowledge that the other realm is available and supports such usage. The use of the home realm MUST be the default unless otherwise configured.
sections.plainLanguage: The realm works like a routing table key. Proxies look it up to decide which server to forward the request to, and they must not rewrite it on the way, or the request would end up in the wrong place.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Since an NAI reveals the home affiliation of a user, it may assist an attacker in further probing the username space. This is of most concern in protocols that transmit the username in clear text across the Internet, such as RADIUS. To prevent snooping of the username, protocols may use confidentiality services provided by the protocols transporting them, such as RADIUS protected by IPsec or Diameter protected by TLS.

This specification adds the possibility of hiding the username part in the NAI by omitting it, which is possible only when NAIs are used together with a separate authentication method that can transfer the username in a secure manner. In some cases application-specific privacy mechanisms have also been used, for instance some EAP methods applying method-specific pseudonyms in the username part of the NAI. Neither approach can protect the realm part, but their advantage over transport protection is that the privacy of the username is protected even through intermediate nodes such as network access servers.

Using the NAI in other protocols has implications for privacy. Any attacker who can observe traffic containing the NAI can track the user and correlate activity across time and across multiple protocols. The authentication credentials therefore SHOULD be transported over channels that permit private communications, or multiple identifiers SHOULD be used so that user tracking is impossible. It is RECOMMENDED that user privacy be enhanced by configuring multiple identifiers for one user, which can be changed over time, though provisioning and management of the identifiers may be difficult in practice.

Multiple identifier formats allow attackers to make contradictory claims without being detected. A close reading of the TTLS specification shows no requirement that inner and outer identifiers be related, so it is valid to use an outer identifier for one example.com and an inner identifier for user@example.org, in which case the request is routed to example.com, which will likely be unable to authenticate user@example.org. A misconfiguration could even proxy the inner request on to the example.org domain, and such cross-domain authentication is highly problematic. It is therefore RECOMMENDED that systems permitting anonymous outer identifiers require the inner domain to be the same as, or a subdomain of, the outer domain, and an authentication request using disparate realms SHOULD be rejected.
sections.plainLanguage: Using one name everywhere is convenient but also means one observer can follow a person around. The RFC accepts that trade-off and recommends that networks protect the credentials in transit, or use several names for the same person.

sections.title: Administration of Names
sections.content:
In order to avoid creating any new administrative procedures, administration of the NAI realm namespace piggybacks on the administration of the DNS namespace. NAI realm names are required to be unique, and the rights to use a given NAI realm for roaming purposes are obtained coincident with acquiring the rights to use a particular fully qualified domain name. Those wishing to use an NAI realm name should first acquire the rights to use the corresponding domain name, and administrators MUST NOT publicly use an NAI realm without first owning the corresponding domain name. Private use of unowned NAI realms within an administrative domain is allowed, though it is RECOMMENDED that example names such as example.com be used.

Using a domain name as the realm does not require the use of DNS to locate the authentication server. While Diameter supports the use of DNS for that purpose, existing RADIUS implementations typically use proxy configuration files to locate authentication servers within a domain and to perform authentication routing. There is also no requirement that the NAI represent a valid email address.
sections.plainLanguage: No new registry is created. If you want to be the home domain for a realm, you need the matching domain name, and the realm is administered exactly like a domain name.

viz.caption: THE ABNF FOR THE NAI AS PRINTED IN RFC 7542

data.title: Network Access Identifier grammar
data.code:
nai            =   utf8-username
nai            =/  "@" utf8-realm
nai            =/  utf8-username "@" utf8-realm

utf8-username  =  dot-string
dot-string     = string *("." string)
string         = 1*utf8-atext

utf8-realm     =  1*( label "." ) label
label          =  utf8-rtext *(ldh-str)
ldh-str        =  *( utf8-rtext / "-" ) utf8-rtext
utf8-rtext     =  ALPHA / DIGIT / UTF8-xtra-char

viz.caption: ILLUSTRATIVE, NOT FROM THE RFC: THE REALM TELLS THE VISITED DOMAIN WHERE TO SEND THE REQUEST
